subject: iot
title: Unit 4 MCQs — IoT Analytics, Security & Privacy

items.q: Which classification of data distinguishes a tabular temperature reading from a video clip?
options: Data in motion vs data at rest
items.explain: Structured data fits a schema/RDBMS (e.g., a temperature value in a known field); unstructured data (text, speech, images, video) has no schema. ~80% of business data is unstructured.

items.q: From an IoT perspective, sensor data travelling through the network toward its destination is:
options: Data in motion (often processed at the edge via fog computing)
items.explain: Smart-object data is 'data in motion' as it transits the network; it's often processed at the edge (fog), then filtered/dropped or forwarded for storage. Data saved to disk/DB is 'at rest'.

items.q: Which analytics type answers 'Why did it happen?'
items.explain: Diagnostic analytics finds the cause of events (via correlation/comparison). Descriptive = what is happening; predictive = what might happen next; prescriptive = what to do about it.

items.q: Recommending 'schedule an oil change and upgrade the cooling system to minimize cost' is which analytics type?
items.explain: Prescriptive analytics goes beyond prediction to recommend optimal actions, weighing cost/benefit/risk. It sits at the top of the complexity/value ladder.

items.q: As you move from descriptive to prescriptive analytics, generally:
options: Both complexity and value increase (predictive/prescriptive rely on ML)
Complexity increases but value stays flat
items.explain: The four types form a rising ladder of complexity AND value. Descriptive/diagnostic use statistics; predictive/prescriptive rely on machine learning and optimization.

items.q: What is the correct order of the IoT analytics pipeline?
options: Storage → Generation → Analytics → Collection → Processing → Action
Generation → Collection → Storage → Processing → Analytics → Visualization/Action
Collection → Generation → Processing → Storage → Action → Analytics
Analytics → Visualization → Storage → Collection → Generation → Processing
items.explain: The six stages: data generation (sensing) → collection (transmission) → storage → processing (clean/transform) → analytics (insight) → visualization & action (decision).

items.q: Which best distinguishes stream processing from batch processing?
options: Stream is for data at rest; batch is for data in motion
Stream processes data in motion in real time (e.g., Spark Streaming/Kafka); batch runs periodic jobs on stored data (e.g., Hadoop)
Batch is always faster than stream
items.explain: Stream processing handles real-time data in motion for immediate reaction; batch processing runs periodic jobs over stored data at rest for deep historical analysis. Many systems use both.

items.q: Which storage type is specifically well-suited to IoT's timestamped sensor readings?
items.explain: Time-series databases (InfluxDB, TimescaleDB) are optimized for timestamped data. NoSQL (MongoDB, Cassandra) suits unstructured data; cloud object stores (S3) handle large-scale archives.

items.q: Machine Learning is best described as:
options: Explicitly programming every rule by hand
A branch of AI that learns patterns from data to make predictions/decisions without explicit programming
items.explain: ML lets computers learn patterns from data and improve with more data, rather than following fixed hand-coded rules — 'learning from experience.'

items.q: Why is the feedback loop important in ML for IoT?
options: Sensors drift and conditions change (model drift), so the model must keep learning from new data to stay accurate
It removes the need for any data
items.explain: ML for IoT isn't train-once. The feedback loop continuously refines the model with fresh data to counter model drift (sensor behavior changing over time) across long deployments.

items.q: Which ML paradigm learns from labeled input-output pairs?
items.explain: Supervised learning trains on labeled examples (features → known target) for classification/regression. Unsupervised finds patterns in unlabeled data; reinforcement learns via rewards/penalties.

items.q: Detecting an unusual vibration surge in a factory machine WITHOUT labeled fault data is an example of:
items.explain: With no labels, anomaly detection (an unsupervised task) flags data points far from normal patterns — ideal for spotting faults/intrusions in raw IoT data. Clustering and dimensionality reduction are the other unsupervised tasks.

items.q: How does an autoencoder detect anomalies in IoT data?
options: It needs labeled fault data for every anomaly type
Trained on normal data, it reconstructs normal patterns with low error; abnormal inputs produce HIGH reconstruction error → anomaly alert
items.explain: An autoencoder learns to compress/reconstruct normal data. Abnormal inputs reconstruct poorly (high error), flagging anomalies without any fault labels — unsupervised anomaly detection.

items.q: An autonomous robot learning navigation by trial and error through rewards and penalties uses:
items.explain: Reinforcement learning learns by interaction — rewards for good outcomes, penalties for bad — suited to sequential decision-making like robot navigation, grid optimization, and drone control.

items.q: In a decision tree, the final classification (e.g., 'Faulty Device') is represented by the:
items.explain: Leaf nodes hold the final classification/prediction. The root is the first question, internal nodes are decisions on attributes, and branches are the outcomes of those decisions.

items.q: A decision tree splits data at each node to maximize:
items.explain: Trees split on the feature giving maximum information gain (largest reduction in entropy/impurity), recursively separating the classes. Entropy measures how 'mixed up' the data is.

items.q: What is 'pruning' in a decision tree, and why do it?
options: Adding more branches to fit training data exactly
Trimming branches to keep the tree from getting too complex — fighting overfitting
items.explain: Pruning trims branches to prevent the tree from becoming overly complex and memorizing noise (overfitting), keeping it general and interpretable.

items.q: Which is the key trade-off between cloud-based and edge-based IoT architectures?
options: Cloud-based is local and low-latency; edge-based is centralized
Cloud-based = centralized, scalable, but latency-bound; edge-based = local, low-latency, offline-resilient, bandwidth-thrifty
They are identical in all respects
items.explain: Cloud-based processes centrally (scalable, global, but round-trip latency, fails offline). Edge-based processes locally (low latency, works offline, saves bandwidth). Most systems are hybrid.

items.q: Which is a key benefit of IoT cloud integration?
options: Eliminates the need for any sensors
Elastic scalability, real-time visibility, predictive analytics, and centralized management with OTA updates
Guarantees zero latency for all devices
items.explain: Cloud integration provides horizontal scalability, real-time data visibility, AI/ML-driven predictive analytics, and secure centralized device management (dashboards, OTA updates, RBAC).

items.q: Which AWS service provides edge computing — local compute and ML inference even when offline?
items.explain: AWS IoT Greengrass runs local computation, ML inference, and analytics at the edge (offline-capable). IoT Core handles device connectivity (MQTT/HTTP/WebSockets); QuickSight visualizes; SageMaker builds ML models.

items.q: Which pairing of AWS and Azure equivalents is correct?
options: AWS IoT Core ≈ Azure IoT Hub (connectivity); AWS Greengrass ≈ Azure IoT Edge (edge compute)
AWS IoT Core ≈ Azure IoT Edge; AWS Greengrass ≈ Azure IoT Hub
Both AWS services are visualization tools
items.explain: IoT Core ≈ IoT Hub for cloud device connectivity; Greengrass ≈ IoT Edge for local/edge compute. Both clouds offer the same cloud-based vs edge-based modes under different names.

items.q: What most distinguishes ThingSpeak (MathWorks) as an IoT platform?
options: It is only for enterprise-scale deployments
Real-time data collection/visualization via channels, with built-in MATLAB analytics — ideal for academic/prototyping projects
items.explain: ThingSpeak collects, analyzes, and visualizes sensor data using channels (8 fields each) and integrates MATLAB analytics in the cloud — a favorite for academic and prototyping IoT projects.

items.q: thinger.io is best characterized as a platform focused on:
options: Device connectivity/management with live read-write of device resources and drag-and-drop dashboards
items.explain: thinger.io centers on device connectivity and management, bidirectional access to device resources/functions, data buckets, and drag-and-drop dashboards — scalable from prototype to production.

items.q: Which security goal is protected primarily by ENCRYPTION?
items.explain: Encryption protects confidentiality (keeping data content unreadable to attackers). Integrity uses hashing; non-repudiation uses digital signatures; availability uses anti-DoS measures.

items.q: Non-repudiation in IoT security ensures that:
options: Data cannot be read by attackers
A party cannot deny having sent a message or the validity of data (primary tool: digital signatures)
items.explain: Non-repudiation prevents a party from denying their action/signature — essential in transactions. Digital signatures combined with other measures provide it.

items.q: A Denial-of-Sleep Attack (DoSA) is IoT-specific because it:
options: Floods a DNS server with traffic
Keeps battery-powered devices awake to drain their power, attacking the power supply and reducing device lifetime until unavailable
items.explain: DoSA targets the power budget of battery devices — preventing sleep (e.g., via a fake device that keeps them transmitting) drains batteries and makes devices unavailable. It exploits IoT's low-power design.

items.q: What makes IoT especially dangerous as a vector for DDoS attacks?
options: There are billions of often-insecure IoT devices (default credentials) that attackers can compromise into a distributed army of 'zombies'
IoT devices cannot connect to networks
items.explain: The massive number of low-security IoT devices can be compromised and coordinated (zombies) to saturate a target simultaneously — the Mirai botnet demonstrated exactly this.

items.q: In a 'black hole attack', the threat actor:
options: Uses a fake device advertising the shortest path, then redirects or silently drops the redirected packets
Adds physical noise to a chip
items.explain: A black hole attack is a routing attack: a fake node claims the shortest path to attract traffic, then drops or redirects it. Defenses include secure L3/L4 protocols (IPSec) and firewalls.

items.q: Zapping a chip's power supply or applying electrostatics to force an insecure boot state is called:
items.explain: Glitch injection adds noise/disturbance (voltage spikes, electrostatics) to push a device outside its safe operating range into an insecure state. Chip makers must add countermeasures (e.g., secure boot).

items.q: Why can data that seems harmless in isolation still pose a privacy risk?
options: When integrated with information from other systems, it may enable identifying or profiling a person
items.explain: Non-sensitive data can become a serious privacy concern once combined with other datasets, enabling re-identification or misuse — which is why de-identification can be undone by integration.

items.q: What does the DREAD risk model stand for?
options: Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users, Discoverability
items.explain: DREAD (Microsoft) rates a threat on Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users, and Discoverability; averaging the scores gives a comparable risk number to prioritize threats.

items.q: Which is the correct order of the threat-modeling process?
options: Rate threats → identify assets → identify message flow → identify threat types
Identify assets → identify message flow → identify threat types → rate threats & calculate risk
Identify threat types → rate threats → identify assets → identify message flow
Identify message flow → rate threats → identify assets → identify threat types
items.explain: Threat modeling: identify assets (and their security needs) → identify message flow → identify threat types → rate threats and calculate risk (e.g., with DREAD).

items.q: An attacker installing a rootkit to gain higher-privilege access to a backend system is which threat type?
items.explain: Escalation of privilege exploits a bug/flaw (e.g., a hidden rootkit) to gain elevated access reserved for higher-privilege users/systems. Spoofing = fake identity; tampering = modify data; disclosure = breach confidentiality.

items.q: A Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) is best described as:
options: A dynamic expert review process to identify, evaluate, and control privacy risks BEFORE issues arise
items.explain: A PIA proactively protects personal information a system collects; it is performed by privacy experts and updated dynamically whenever the system changes. Principles: minimize collection, consent, opt-out, delete when done.

items.q: The IoT Cybersecurity Improvement Act (2020) requires vendors to ensure devices:
options: Have no known vulnerabilities, use advanced protocols, contain NO hard-coded credentials, and provide incident notifications
Collect as much data as possible
items.explain: The CSIA (for US federal buildings) mandates no known vulnerabilities, advanced protocols, no hard-coded credentials, and security-incident notifications — legislating against the weaknesses that enabled attacks like Mirai.

items.q: The 2016 Mirai botnet attack primarily violated which security goal, and how?
options: Availability — by infecting default-credential IoT devices and using them as a DDoS army against Dyn
items.explain: Mirai compromised IoT devices with hard-coded/default credentials (cameras, gateways) into a botnet, launching a DDoS that disrupted Dyn's DNS and 13,000+ domains — an attack on availability.

items.q: The TRENDnet webcam incident (sending login info unencrypted, storing it in clear text) is a classic violation of:
items.explain: Transmitting credentials without encryption and storing them in clear text (plus a bug exposing video) violated confidentiality — anyone knowing the IP could view the feed.

items.q: Which blockchain property most directly addresses IoT data-tampering (integrity) concerns?
options: Immutability — hash-linked blocks make any tampering with past records evident
items.explain: Blockchain's immutability (each block cryptographically links to the previous) means altering past data breaks the hash chain and is detectable — directly countering tampering and providing auditable provenance.

items.q: What is the fundamental tension between blockchain and IoT devices?
options: Blockchains are too simple for IoT
Blockchains are compute-, storage-, and energy-hungry (esp. Proof-of-Work), while IoT devices are constrained, low-power, and battery-limited
items.explain: Classic blockchains demand heavy compute/storage/energy and have low throughput/high latency — a poor fit for constrained, battery-powered IoT nodes. This drives lightweight, IoT-tailored ledgers and offloading to gateways/cloud.

items.q: How does blockchain help remove a single point of failure in IoT?
options: By adding one powerful central server
Its decentralized ledger is replicated across many nodes, so there is no central server to attack or take down
items.explain: Decentralization replicates the ledger across nodes, eliminating reliance on a single central cloud/server — improving availability and letting devices verify data among themselves without a trusted middleman.
